sections.title: Source findings — Kirknewton household check, 20 October 2026
sections.markdown:
The Findmypast transcripts inspected on 20 October 2026 name William Glasgow as father of Bessie (21 April 1682), John (29 November 1702) and William (22 April 1705), all at Kirknewton and East Calder. None displays a mother, residence within the parish, occupation or witnesses. Bessie’s transcript gives OPR 689/20, item 1, page 39; the two later transcripts give the same archive reference and item but no page. This provider reference differs from the supplied ScotlandsPeople parish 690 references and must be reconciled against the original. No original register image was inspected.

The FamilySearch citations previously used to say William and Ann McCook were both recorded as parents were also inspected. VQ4K-ZQN is the father entry for Bessie, linked to child VQ4K-ZQF; it names William only. VQ4K-FY9 records the child William Glasgou and his father William, without a mother. Both display “Image Unavailable”. These indexes therefore do not establish Ann’s maternity or the couple’s marriage. The older claim that those citations name Ann is superseded; the earlier attached family and all citations remain available for comparison. An omitted mother is not evidence excluding Ann.

Retain Ann McCook’s existing spouse and maternal attachments as unproved tree claims; no person is detached or redated. The three same-name father entries do not alone establish one continuous 1682–1705 household. They supply no bridge to the older John Glasgow-3610’s Easter Newtoun household, so the selected John-to-William father hypothesis remains uncertain at 24%. The 1702 transcript supports 29 November as its baptism date, but does not resolve John-1544’s separate before-11-November field; no vital field is changed. This is a source-scope correction, not a new baptism discovery, father selection, confidence upgrade or component join.

Inspect the original OPR entries for residence, maternal wording and witnesses, and seek an independently sourced William/Ann marriage or family record. Preserve the distinction between a father explicitly named in a child record and identification of that father across later households.

potential_parentage.method: Automated leads use birth surnames—not married surnames—as parental eligibility, role-specific biological age limits, bounded and approximate-date uncertainty, household chronology, specific time-aware localities, mapped distance, tenancy succession, migration destinations and sex-aware Scottish naming positions across generations. People already attached as the subject's parents stay in the identity summary and are excluded from this alternative-candidate list, regardless of relationship confidence. The main calibration uses clues available on disconnected profiles; existing parent and sibling links are retained as comparison context rather than treated as transferable evidence. Common ordered names and grandparent-to-child echoes receive a small non-zero weight, so a John or James match can support several independent criteria without producing a lead alone. Rare names, repeated bearers and bundles across otherwise distinct branches receive substantially more weight according to catalogue frequency. An exact migration place is weighted by its rarity and repetition across both branches; a shared destination country is worth only one point. Extra weight is added only when at least three independent clue types converge: naming, locality, specific migration, household chronology or collateral networks. Sparse profiles retain a clearly labelled chronology-only fallback instead of disappearing. Countries, states, counties and research clusters do not count as a shared locality, and fallback, broad representative or kin-inferred coordinates are excluded from distance scoring. Shared descendant profiles are removed before branch-name comparison. A candidate already recorded as a parent-in-law is excluded. A confident or independently supported parent is treated as settled; uncertain and unassessed attachments remain open to alternative comparison. A different linked parent, an uncle/aunt or grandparent path, and a matching existing child profile prevent an alternative from being classified as a strong direct-parent lead until the underlying tree conflict or duplicate is resolved. Familiar forms such as Bessie are normalised. Surname remains an eligibility filter worth zero points.
potential_parentage.warning: Naming customs, shared farms and occupations are circumstantial. Children, spouses and collateral relatives may be missing, and tree-derived family networks are not independent evidence. Scores rank research leads; they do not prove parentage.

assessment_history.previous_notes: The maintained reading of PRONI T1959/3 describes the writer’s paternal grandfather William Glasgow of Killycurragh and his wife, an unidentified Miss Cunningham of Omagh. Their sons included James and Samuel, who remained on the family farm; Samuel occupied the parental house. The writer’s father was the minister who died in July 1801. This is an undated, unsigned family recollection known through a published transcription, not an original newly inspected in this review. An earlier HTTP 403 check failed; the published transcription was subsequently read in the browser on 20 October 2026. The original letter remains uninspected. The percentages assess each entire father-to-profile proposition, including identification of the named son with the later profile; they are subjective comparative judgments, not measured frequencies. The original letter and holding succession remain unverified. Samuel’s circa-1800 birth is an estimate, and a materially older Samuel or a later same-name descendant is possible. His wife Anne’s approximate 1801 birth and their children in the 1820s–1830s do not date Samuel himself. A nephew or later tenant could share the name and townland. Do not transfer a recorded relationship to a later adult merely from the letter’s parent clause. William’s birth and death remain unknown. The letter names an older William as his father; the specific Kirknewton profile is a 36% possibility. His mother remains unidentified. Miss Cunningham is retained as William’s reported wife, without selecting her as either profile’s mother. No existing person is merged or redated, and no live WikiTree edit has been made.

record_associations.note: The anonymous family recollection printed by Faris on p.9 explicitly gives James Glasgow, husband of Margaret Rutherford, four sons: William, Robert, James who settled near Moneymore, and Samuel who went to America, plus daughter Ellen. The letter-defined father is the family role represented by James-1025. These are specific named relationships, substantially stronger than the contributed-tree and locality summaries used by the earlier percentages. The same full-letter tradition was already read on 20 October; actual Faris pages now confirm its full structure. Its reproduction by Albert Rutherford and Faris’s pedigree are dependent presentations, not independent witnesses. Father James-1025, specifically the James/Margaret Rutherford family-account role: James-1024 18%→78%, Samuel-1492 23%→76%, Robert-2425 18%→77%, William-2426 46%→84%, all now probable. The American Robert-12/Arthur-649/Joseph-1543 father grades remain35%, John-4027 remains30%, Mary-4030 remains22%; James-1025’s own William-1026 father remains32%. These are probable, not confident, relationships reconstructed from an anonymous retrospective family recollection, with no newly inspected parent register. The original letter remains uninspected. Faris calls the anonymous recollection file5 within PRONI T1959, while Rutherford’s reproduced copy cites T1959/3; retain this reference discrepancy pending archive checking. The 1759 probate index says Drumcarn and names no kin; neither that testator nor the inherited life dates are identified by this reassessment. The letter calls William eldest although the imported sibling birth estimates put him later; those estimates remain unverified. Faris also flags Samuel’s infant daughter and surviving mother-in-law in1824 against the supposed early paternal death. Those tensions require testing, not automatic exclusion. Preserve all existing people, vital fields, maternal grades and alternatives. No Scottish migration, identity merge, live edit or new father attachment is claimed.
